My guests today are Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital, and Geoffrey Canada, founder of Harlem Children's Zone. Geoffrey spent decades helping disadvantaged kids get a great education, but it takes more than that to achieve the American dream. Without savings, you’re one emergency away from bankruptcy.

 Brad set out to change that. When he first called me about Invest America in 2020, I thought it was a fool’s errand. Six years later, nearly 70 million children have accounts in their name, and every American newborn receives $1,000 in the S&P 500. The challenge now is getting families to claim their accounts, since free money is surprisingly hard to give away.

 Brad and Geoffrey believe even a small nest egg, when given a head start on compounding, can help rebuild faith in capitalism. As AI reshapes the economy, they see these accounts as the basis of a new social contract built on ownership and participation, where every child owns a piece of the upside.

 Please enjoy my conversation with Brad and Geoffrey.

For roughly 25 years, the economics of the web were pretty straightforward. Publishers created information, Google indexed it, users searched Google, Google sent those users to those publishers’ websites, and the publishers monetized those visits with advertising. But last month, the stock of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, plunged nearly $500 billion when the company flagged to investors that the firm would use more AI in its search.

 The rise of AI doesn’t just threaten to disrupt Google; it threatens to destroy the economics of web publishing. With AI, Google doesn’t just direct our attention to the answer; it now answers the question entirely. For many publishers that live and die on search traffic and clicks, this shift is existential. News websites are shuttering, journalism layoffs are rising, and even Wikipedia reported that human page views have fallen by almost 10 percent in the last year. Artificial intelligence is very much threatening to change the business model of the internet as we understand it, and an internet that runs on chatbots is going to require a totally new set of economic rules.

Michael Rubin is the founder and CEO of Fanatics . He grew up outside Philadelphia, started tuning skis at 12, opened a ski shop in his parents' basement at 13, and had a storefront in a shopping center by 14. At 16, after a winter without snow, he was facing $200,000 in bills and thought he was going bankrupt, until he learned minors can't legally take on debt. He settled for $35,000, then bought a bankrupt store's $200,000 of inventory for $13,000. That deal got him into the closeout business, and by 21 he was doing $150 million a year. Michael tells the story of nearly being margined out of GSI Commerce during the 2009 financial crisis, with hours to spare, two years before eBay bought it for $2.4 billion. He explains how Fanatics grew from a fan gear business into a $14 billion digital sports platform with 140 million customers, why he guaranteed the leagues the high watermark of a cyclical trading card market, and how debut patches and George Condo–painted cards turned collectibles into "art for sports fans." He also shares the advice Robert Kraft gave him when a partner broke a deal, why he gave investors their money back on NFTs and Mitchell & Ness, why there's a "0.0 chance" he'd put his own money into prediction markets at today's valuations, and the call from Silver Lake's Greg Mondre that saved him from a multibillion-dollar mistake.

 Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, 1993–2026 

 Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday, November 12, 2026. He had been CEO of the company ever since he founded it on April 5, 1993. Nvidia started out as a graphics card company; Huang’s exit — nominally because of affairs with a buyer who may or may not have been a Chinese spy, as well as at least two company employees — was ultimately because Nvidia was, by the powers that be, considered a defense contractor, and Huang never adjusted.

 In this, Huang was the ultimate victim of his own success. Nvidia’s first graphics cards simply translated triangles into pixels. The 2001 GeForce 3 introduced a programmable pixel shader, which meant a video card’s functionality was no longer pre-defined. The killer move, however — which almost killed the company — was the 2006 introduction of CUDA, which was an API for programming those shaders. For much of the next 16 years Huang sold the gospel of CUDA , convinced it was the platform for a future of accelerated computing; then, in 2022, came ChatGPT.

 ChatGPT made clear what GPUs were most useful for: large language models, and Nvidia made the best GPUs.
